query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a minor glass‐forming element (e.g., Si) with Ta in multiprincipal‐element alloys promotes the in situ formation of a composite oxide scale (Ta2O5–SiO2) that passivates the surface and limits oxygen ingress.
generation.material_initial_state: A multiprincipal‐element alloy with a conventional composition lacking sufficient glass‐forming constituents, wherein Ta is present at a level insufficient to form a continuous, protective oxide on its own.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy composition to include a controlled minor addition of Si (e.g., 1–3 at.%) along with an intermediate Ta level (around 10–15 at.%), so that during oxidation, Si oxidizes in tandem with Ta.
generation.conditions: Prepare alloys with identical base compositions but with and without the Si addition; subject all samples to isothermal oxidation in air at temperatures ranging from 800 °C to 1400 °C for fixed durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a composite, viscous oxide scale comprised of Ta2O5 and SiO2 that adheres well to the substrate.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures the minor Si addition oxidizes concurrently with Ta. SiO2, a known glass‐forming oxide, combines with Ta2O5 to form a continuous, low‐permeability, composite oxide scale. This scale obstructs oxygen diffusion more effectively than Ta2O5 alone, addressing the absence of a natural B2O3 analog in metallic systems. The mechanism builds on the paper’s demonstration that a Ta‐induced oxide layer can reduce oxidation, but modifies it to suit conventional alloys by providing a glass‐forming partner.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with both Ta and a minor Si addition are expected to show a lower oxidation mass gain and a smoother, more adherent oxide scale compared to alloys containing Ta alone or no Si. The improvement should be observable across the tested temperature range.
generation.baseline: Multiprincipal‐element alloys containing Ta without a supplementary glass‐forming element, which under similar conditions form patchy or less protective oxide scales.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis should hold for alloy compositions where the added Si remains in solid solution and does not lead to deleterious silicide formation; excessive Si may form brittle phases. The beneficial composite oxide is anticipated only when the Si level is maintained below a few atomic percent.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., mass gain reduction) and the optimum Si content need to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical multiprincipal‐element alloy samples: one set with the controlled Si addition (1–3 at.%) alongside an optimized Ta level (10–15 at.%) and the other set with only the Ta addition. Oxidize all samples at 800, 1200, and 1400 °C for the same duration. Use SEM, EDS, and XPS to characterize the oxide scale and continuously measure oxidation mass gain.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area over time/temperature.
Morphology and continuity of the oxide scale via electron microscopy.
Chemical composition and phase identification of the oxide scale.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the Si addition do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., reduced mass gain and improved oxide scale continuity) compared to the Ta‐only samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

paper_did: Synthesized equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloys (and a variant with ~6 at.% Al replacing Mn) via arc melting, homogenization, cold rolling, and recrystallization.
Conducted controlled oxidation experiments at 400 °C in 10 mbar O2 (with exposures from as short as 2 min to 120 min) on both the baseline alloy and the Al-modified alloy.

Applied in situ atom probe tomography (APT), transmission electron microscopy (TEM), grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS), and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy to track compositional and structural evolution of the oxide layers.

Characterized a layered oxide structure in the baseline alloy (Ni-enriched pre-oxide, Cr-rich inner oxide, and Fe/Co/Mn-rich outer oxide) and observed that introducing Al altered the oxide layering by creating an Al-enriched interface along with Cr-, Mn-, Co-, and Fe-dominated regions.
paper_reported: The paper reported that oxidation of the CoCrFeNiMn alloy follows a sequence determined by element-specific diffusivity and redox potential, with early oxidation dominated by Cr and Mn, later transition to Fe and Co at the outer surface, and the formation of compositionally distinct layered oxide films.

It showed that in situ APT and complementary TEM and GIWAXS data reveal non-uniform, three‐dimensional oxide structures and that the preferential interactivity parameter (PIP) can be used to predict oxidation behavior in these complex alloys.

For the Al-modified alloy, the study observed an additional complexity: an Al enrichment at the metal/oxide interface that appears to influence subsequent formation of a Cr-rich inner oxide and modified outer oxide layers, with associated changes in oxidation states (e.g., Mn and Fe shifting in oxidation behavior in the presence of Al).
paper_proposed: The study proposes that a mechanistic understanding of element-specific oxidation—including both kinetic and thermodynamic factors codified by the PIP—can pave the way for predictive design of high-entropy alloys with improved oxidation resistance.

It suggests that further exploration of the interplay between alloying elements, diffusion kinetics, and oxide scale formation may enable tailored interventions (such as altering alloy composition) to enhance high-temperature performance under extreme conditions.

hypotheses.material_initial_state: An equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn multiprincipal-element alloy in a supersaturated solid solution state.
hypotheses.intervention: Substitute a small fraction (~5–6 at.%) of one of the more rapidly diffusing elements (e.g., Mn) with Al during alloy synthesis.
hypotheses.conditions: Oxidation treatment at 400 °C in a controlled oxygen atmosphere (10 mbar O2) over extended times (up to 120 min).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, coherent, ultrathin Al2O3 sublayer that acts as a diffusion barrier, followed by the conventional Cr-rich oxide growth on top.
hypotheses.mechanism: Because Al has a smaller atomic radius (rAl = 184 pm) and a lower standard reduction potential (EAl3+/Al0 = −1.67) compared to other constituents, it oxidizes first and establishes a dense, stable Al2O3 layer. This sublayer restricts further cation diffusion (especially Cr and Mn) and decouples the kinetics of subsequent oxidation layers. The duplex oxide (inner Al2O3 and outer Cr2O3) improves oxidation resistance by reducing the oxide growth rate and delaying spallation as observed via in situ APT and X-ray techniques in the paper (e.g., see PMC11169556::web::015).
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, the Al-modified alloy should exhibit a thinner overall oxide scale, lower weight gain during high-temperature oxidation, and a more continuous and adherent oxide layer. The controlled Al layer is predicted to lower further diffusion-driven oxidation by at least a modest percent, relative to unmodified HEA behavior under identical conditions.
hypotheses.baseline: The unmodified equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy that develops a multilayer oxide with distinct Cr-, Mn-, Fe-, and Co-rich regions as described in PMC11169556::web::002 and subsequent sections.
hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism should hold under oxidation temperatures up to roughly 500 °C–700 °C where the protective alumina phase remains stable. At temperatures significantly above 900 °C, volatile oxides (e.g., CrO3) and other competing effects might override the barrier effect.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The precise minimal amount of Al needed for an optimal continuous oxide sublayer and its long-term stability under cyclic conditions remain to be precisely quantified.

hypotheses.material_initial_state: An equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy with a conventional, recrystallized microstructure obtainable via standard annealing.

hypotheses.conditions: Maintain oxidation at 400 °C under 10 mbar O2 over a range of times sufficient to monitor early and later stage oxidation (e.g., 2 min to 120 min).
hypotheses.structural_mediator: Grain boundary density and oxide scale uniformity at the metal/oxide interface.
hypotheses.mechanism: While grain boundaries typically act as high-diffusivity pathways, when an adherent oxide begins to form, a high density of grain boundaries can promote rapid lateral coalescence of the nascent oxide and also act as nucleation sites for a uniform, continuous protective oxide. In the refined-grain alloy, the high density of nucleation sites could enable early closure of diffusion paths, reducing the overall oxidation rate. Conversely, coarse grains may lead to localized fast diffusion paths that accelerate the oxidation process. This builds on the idea of diffusion-mediated oxidation seen in the paper, recalibrating grain size as a key parameter.
hypotheses.predicted_outcome: The refined-grained alloy is predicted to form a more uniform and adherent oxide scale with slower overall growth than its coarse-grained counterpart. For example, weight gain and oxide thickness measurements should be lower for the nano-grained sample over a 120-min oxidation period.
hypotheses.baseline: The standard recrystallized alloy with moderate grain size obtained via typical 50% cold rolling and annealing, as described in PMC11169556::web::020.
hypotheses.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for oxidation temperatures where grain boundary diffusion significantly impacts kinetics (likely in the moderate range of 400 °C to 600 °C). At very high temperatures, accelerated diffusion might blur the effect.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The exact balance between enhanced nucleation (beneficial) and potentially increased diffusion along grain boundaries (detrimental) introduces uncertainty in predicting net oxidation kinetics.

paper_did: Synthesized equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloys (and a variant with partial Al substitution for Mn) via arc melting, homogenization annealing, cold rolling, and recrystallization to obtain a single-phase FCC structure.

Subjected samples to oxidation at 400 °C in a controlled oxygen atmosphere (approximately 10 mbar O2) for varying durations (from as short as 2 minutes up to 120 minutes) using both in situ and ex situ setups.

Applied advanced characterization techniques—including in situ atom probe tomography (APT), cross‐sectional transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with STEM-EDS, grazing incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering (GIWAXS), and X-ray absorption near edge spectroscopy (XANES)—to monitor oxide scale formation, elemental segregation, and compositional layering.

Developed and used the preferential interactivity parameter (PIP) to predict and rationalize the layered, compositionally distinct oxide growth (e.g., Ni-rich pre-oxide, Cr-rich inner oxide, and outer oxides enriched in Fe, Mn, and Co) and analyzed how elemental interactions (and later, Al addition) affect oxidation mechanisms.
paper_reported: Layered oxide scales form during oxidation at 400 °C, with an initial Ni-enriched pre-oxide layer, followed by a Cr-rich inner oxide and an outer oxide enriched in Fe, Mn, and Co; the oxide scale morphology is non-uniform with features such as Co-enriched islands.

The oxidation sequence is governed by a combination of thermodynamics (redox potentials, atomic radii, cohesive energy density) and kinetic factors (diffusion processes, defect and vacancy formation), as interpreted via the preferential interactivity parameter (PIP).

The oxidation process evolves through changing regimes (from Cabrera–Mott to Xu-Rosso-Bruemmer) and later-stage thermo-oxidative composition inversion (TOCI) that rearranges the oxide scale structure.

Addition of Al (at approximately 6 at.%, replacing part of Mn) alters the oxidation pattern by promoting the formation of an extra oxide layer and modifying the elemental interactions (evidenced by changes in oxidation states in XANES), underscoring the sensitive interplay between composition and oxidation behavior.
paper_proposed: To leverage the mechanistic insights and the PIP framework for the predictive design of complex high‐entropy or multiprincipal‐element alloys with improved resistance to oxidation under extreme conditions.
To further explore how variations in elemental composition and processing conditions can tune interfacial diffusion, defect formation, and ultimately the stability and adherence of oxide scales.
To utilize advanced microscopy and spectroscopy techniques to better understand the role of interfacial chemistry and microstructural heterogeneities in controlling oxidation pathways.

hypotheses.mechanism: Y is known in superalloys to promote the reactive element effect. The low solubility and high interfacial activity of Y drive its segregation to grain boundaries of the nascent oxide. This segregation reduces void formation and local interfacial strain, hindering rapid cation diffusion and spallation, thus stabilizing the oxide scale. It leverages the interplay between interfacial diffusional kinetics and oxidation-driven defect formation described in the paper.

hypotheses.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for oxidation in the temperature range up to about 500–600 °C, where the reactive element effect is active; at very high temperatures (>700–800 °C), volatile oxide formation or rapid diffusion may diminish the beneficial impact.
hypotheses.uncertainty: The optimal amount of Y and its distribution dynamics in the complex alloy matrix may present variability; interactions with other elements in the HEA could influence the segregation kinetics unpredictably.

This interplay of accelerated nucleation and controlled growth can improve oxidation resistance.

paper_did: Designed and fabricated a novel Y‐ and Hf‐co‐doped NiCoCrAl‐type multi‐principal element alloy (MPEA) (Ni32Co25Cr25Al18) using conventional arc melting, yielding a eutectic dual‐phase (γ/β) microstructure with a pronounced lamellar morphology in the β‐phase.

Employed CALPHAD calculations and validated these predictions using XRD, SEM, TEM, and STEM‐EDS mapping, which confirmed the dual-phase (γ/β) structure and revealed nanoscale Cr‐rich (α‐Cr) precipitates in the MPEA.

Conducted high‐temperature oxidation tests at 1200°C (both isothermal for 500 h and cyclic oxidation tests), quantifying oxidation kinetics (mass gain and rate constant), TGO (thermally grown oxide) thickness, and spallation behavior.
Assessed the mechanical properties (tensile strength and elongation) of the MPEA versus a conventional NiCoCrAlY alloy.

Characterized lattice distortion in the Al‐depletion zone (ADZ) using high‐resolution TEM, geometric phase analysis (GPA), and first‐principles calculations to correlate the enhanced oxidation resistance with suppressed Al diffusion.
paper_reported: The MPEA exhibited a 59% reduction in oxidation rate constant (1.28 × 10^−12 g² cm⁻⁴ s⁻¹) compared to the conventional NiCoCrAlY alloy (3.11 × 10^−12 g² cm⁻⁴ s⁻¹), along with forming a thinner, continuous Al₂O₃ scale (8.04 µm vs. 11.25 µm) with negligible spallation (<2%).

The superior oxidation resistance was attributed to the dual benefits of a refined eutectic lamellar microstructure that promotes rapid and exclusive Al₂O₃ formation, and lattice distortion–induced diffusion suppression in the ADZ that retards sustained oxide growth.
Enhanced mechanical performance (higher ultimate tensile strength and ductility) was observed in the MPEA relative to conventional NiCoCrAlY.

Nanoscale α‐Cr precipitates observed in the β‐phase were identified as beneficial for providing structurally compatible nucleation sites (via transformation to Cr₂O₃) that accelerate the formation of a coherent, protective α‐Al₂O₃ scale.
paper_proposed: The paper introduces a dual‐strategy design paradigm, combining tailored eutectic microstructural control and lattice distortion–induced diffusion suppression, as a new route for designing next‐generation thermal barrier coating bond coats capable of ultra‐stable oxidation resistance at 1200°C.

While detailed future processing strategies were not explicitly outlined, the study suggests that further mechanistic investigations into oxide scale evolution, diffusion barrier optimization, and the interplay of microstructure with oxidation kinetics can inform improved bond coat designs.

paper_did: Produced an AlNbTiVZr0.25 refractory high‐entropy alloy by arc melting and homogenization at 1200 °C, followed by specimen preparation via machining and surface polishing.
Conducted isothermal oxidation experiments in static lab air at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 100 h and at 900 °C for 50 h, with intermittent mass measurements.

Characterized the oxidized samples using X‐ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, energy‐dispersive spectroscopy, and cross‐sectional imaging to analyze oxide scale composition, morphology, and oxidation kinetics.
paper_reported: Observed two-stage oxidation kinetics at 600–700 °C, with an initial nearly parabolic mass gain (n ≈ 0.46–0.48) transitioning to a faster, breakaway oxidation stage (n ≈ 0.72–0.75); at 800 °C nearly linear oxidation (n ≈ 0.92) was seen, and at 900 °C the sample disintegrated after 50 h.

pool.builds_on: The paper demonstrated that surface speciation and interfacial chemistry govern the oxide growth in multiprincipal-element alloys. This hypothesis takes that insight further by leveraging reactive element effects—commonly used in superalloys—to engineer the oxide scale through dopant-driven interfacial segregation.
pool.what_is_new: This approach introduces a controlled reactive element doping strategy (not merely altering elemental proportions as in the paper) to form an improved, segregation-aided oxide barrier, thereby explicitly targeting the kinetics and adhesion of the oxide scale in HEAs under high-temperature oxidation.

fields.hypothesis: Incorporating a minor reactive element dopant (e.g., ~1 at.% Y) into the multiprincipal‐element alloy to enhance oxide scale adhesion and resistance through reactive element segregation at oxide grain boundaries.
fields.material_initial_state: An equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy produced by conventional arc melting and homogenization with a single-phase FCC structure.
fields.intervention: Introduce ~1 at.% yttrium (Y) into the alloy composition during synthesis.
fields.conditions: Expose samples to oxidation at 400 °C in a controlled oxygen atmosphere (around 10 mbar O2) for varying durations (e.g., 30–120 min).
fields.structural_mediator: Segregation of Y to the metal/oxide interface and within oxide grain boundaries, leading to a more coherent and adherent, fine-grained oxide scale.
fields.mechanism: Y is known in superalloys to promote the reactive element effect. The low solubility and high interfacial activity of Y drive its segregation to grain boundaries of the nascent oxide. This segregation reduces void formation and local interfacial strain, hindering rapid cation diffusion and spallation, thus stabilizing the oxide scale. It leverages the interplay between interfacial diffusional kinetics and oxidation-driven defect formation described in the paper.
fields.predicted_outcome: The Y-doped alloy should form a thinner, more uniform, and better-adherent oxide scale compared to the undoped baseline. Expected measurable improvements include reduced weight gain during oxidation and enhanced resistance to spallation (possibly on the order of a modest reduction in oxide thickness, although the precise magnitude is uncertain).
fields.baseline: The standard equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn alloy without Y addition, which exhibits multi-layered oxide growth as detailed in PMC11169556::web::002 and following sections.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for oxidation in the temperature range up to about 500–600 °C, where the reactive element effect is active; at very high temperatures (>700–800 °C), volatile oxide formation or rapid diffusion may diminish the beneficial impact.
fields.uncertainty: The optimal amount of Y and its distribution dynamics in the complex alloy matrix may present variability; interactions with other elements in the HEA could influence the segregation kinetics unpredictably.

Characterize the oxide scale via cross‐sectional TEM, measure weight gain, and perform adhesion/spallation tests.

Weight gain during oxidation
Adhesion strength tests or spallation assessments

pool.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes to manipulate the β-phase morphology by processing (directional solidification) to further enhance oxidation resistance, a processing route and mechanistic link that was not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Enhancing the lamellar β‐phase morphology by directional solidification increases the β‐phase aspect ratio, which lowers the number of phase intercepts (PL) per unit length and thus reduces the effective critical Al concentration needed for exclusive Al2O3 formation. This microstructural tailoring is expected to accelerate the formation of a continuous, protective alumina scale and reduce long‐term oxidation rates.
fields.material_initial_state: A NiCoCrAl‐type MPEA produced by conventional arc melting that exhibits a eutectic dual-phase (γ/β) microstructure with a moderate β‐phase aspect ratio.
fields.intervention: Apply directional solidification during processing to produce a more refined, highly lamellar microstructure with an increased β‐phase aspect ratio.
fields.conditions: Isothermal oxidation testing at 1200°C under controlled cyclic oxidation conditions, with identical compositions aside from the processing route.
fields.structural_mediator: Increased lamellar β‐phase aspect ratio that reduces the effective PL, thereby lowering the critical Al concentration for maintaining exclusive Al2O3 formation on the surface.
fields.mechanism: A higher aspect ratio of the β‐phase limits the number of phase boundaries per unit length, effectively reducing the local Al-depletion rate and aiding rapid formation of a continuous Al2O3 scale. The reduction in phase intersections mitigates Al flux discrepancies and local compositional heterogeneities, slowing further oxide growth and improving scale adherence.
fields.predicted_outcome: Samples with a tailored high-aspect-ratio lamellar structure will exhibit lower oxidation rate constants and thinner, more coherent oxide scales (with reduced spallation) relative to the baseline, with improvements potentially on the order of an additional 20-30% reduction in oxidation kinetics, within the uncertainty of scale formation kinetics.
fields.baseline: The performance of the arc-melted MPEA with the original eutectic microstructure, as characterized in the paper.
fields.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for alloys where the phase chemistry and overall composition remain in the eutectic regime; if the β-phase becomes too scarce or if the aspect ratio cannot be meaningfully increased, the effect may not be observed.
fields.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in oxidation rate constants depend on the achievable aspect ratios and may vary; detailed thermal profiles during directional solidification must be optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MPEA samples: one using conventional arc melting and one using directional solidification to obtain a high-aspect-ratio lamellar structure. Expose both to identical oxidation testing at 1200°C for 500 h.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directionally solidified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >15-20% improvement) in oxidation rate constant and TGO spallation relative to the baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

fields.hypothesis: Minor Nb substitution in the multiprincipal-element alloy further increases lattice distortion in the Al-depletion zone, thereby elevating vacancy formation energies and cation migration barriers. fields.material_initial_state: A baseline NiCoCrAl-type MPEA with dual-phase (γ/β) eutectic microstructure and demonstrated oxidation resistance at 1200°C as reported in the paper.
fields.intervention: Introduce a small substitutional addition (approximately 2 at.%) of Nb in place of a portion of Cr in the alloy composition.

fields.uncertainty: The exact impact of a 2 at.% Nb addition on vacancy formation energies and diffusion rates is not precisely known and requires systematic investigation.

fields.boundary: The mechanism should hold for alloys where grain boundary diffusion is the dominant transport mechanism and where the intrinsic diffusivities of the passivating elements are high relative to competing elements; extreme grain size reductions beyond a critical limit may introduce additional defects that could counteract improvements.
fields.uncertainty: Precise quantitative benefits (e.g., percentage reduction in oxide thickness) depend on the exact grain size, alloy composition, and test conditions.

top3.label: C13
top3.builds_on: The paper’s finding that Ta addition can form a protective Ta2O5-based oxide layer in ceramics; here the mechanism is extended to metallic alloys by supplementing with a glass‐forming oxide component.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces the co‐addition of a minor glass‐forming element (Si) in multiprincipal‐element alloys to create a composite oxide scale (Ta2O5–SiO2), overcoming the limitation that conventional alloys lack the B2O3 component present in the ceramic system.

fields.hypothesis: Integrating a minor glass‐forming element (e.g., Si) with Ta in multiprincipal‐element alloys promotes the in situ formation of a composite oxide scale (Ta2O5–SiO2) that passivates the surface and limits oxygen ingress.
fields.material_initial_state: A multiprincipal‐element alloy with a conventional composition lacking sufficient glass‐forming constituents, wherein Ta is present at a level insufficient to form a continuous, protective oxide on its own.
fields.intervention: Modify the alloy composition to include a controlled minor addition of Si (e.g., 1–3 at.%) along with an intermediate Ta level (around 10–15 at.%), so that during oxidation, Si oxidizes in tandem with Ta.
fields.conditions: Prepare alloys with identical base compositions but with and without the Si addition; subject all samples to isothermal oxidation in air at temperatures ranging from 800 °C to 1400 °C for fixed durations.
fields.structural_mediator: The formation of a composite, viscous oxide scale comprised of Ta2O5 and SiO2 that adheres well to the substrate.
fields.mechanism: At high temperatures the minor Si addition oxidizes concurrently with Ta. SiO2, a known glass‐forming oxide, combines with Ta2O5 to form a continuous, low‐permeability, composite oxide scale. This scale obstructs oxygen diffusion more effectively than Ta2O5 alone, addressing the absence of a natural B2O3 analog in metallic systems. The mechanism builds on the paper’s demonstration that a Ta‐induced oxide layer can reduce oxidation, but modifies it to suit conventional alloys by providing a glass‐forming partner.
fields.predicted_outcome: Alloys with both Ta and a minor Si addition are expected to show a lower oxidation mass gain and a smoother, more adherent oxide scale compared to alloys containing Ta alone or no Si. The improvement should be observable across the tested temperature range.
fields.baseline: Multiprincipal‐element alloys containing Ta without a supplementary glass‐forming element, which under similar conditions form patchy or less protective oxide scales.
fields.boundary: The hypothesis should hold for alloy compositions where the added Si remains in solid solution and does not lead to deleterious silicide formation; excessive Si may form brittle phases. The beneficial composite oxide is anticipated only when the Si level is maintained below a few atomic percent.
fields.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., mass gain reduction) and the optimum Si content need to be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical multiprincipal‐element alloy samples: one set with the controlled Si addition (1–3 at.%) alongside an optimized Ta level (10–15 at.%) and the other set with only the Ta addition. Oxidize all samples at 800, 1200, and 1400 °C for the same duration. Use SEM, EDS, and XPS to characterize the oxide scale and continuously measure oxidation mass gain.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area over time/temperature.
Morphology and continuity of the oxide scale via electron microscopy.
Chemical composition and phase identification of the oxide scale.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the Si addition do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in oxidation resistance (e.g., reduced mass gain and improved oxide scale continuity) compared to the Ta‐only samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

top3.label: C2
top3.builds_on: the finding that the eutectic lamellar structure in the MPEA accelerates exclusive Al2O3 scale formation via optimized Al supply, as discussed in the paper.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes to manipulate the β-phase morphology by processing (directional solidification) to further enhance oxidation resistance, a processing route and mechanistic link that was not explored in the paper.

fields.hypothesis: Enhancing the lamellar β‐phase morphology by directional solidification increases the β‐phase aspect ratio, which lowers the number of phase intercepts (PL) per unit length and thus reduces the effective critical Al concentration needed for exclusive Al2O3 formation. This microstructural tailoring is expected to accelerate the formation of a continuous, protective alumina scale and reduce long‐term oxidation rates.
fields.material_initial_state: A NiCoCrAl‐type MPEA produced by conventional arc melting that exhibits a eutectic dual-phase (γ/β) microstructure with a moderate β‐phase aspect ratio.
fields.intervention: Apply directional solidification during processing to produce a more refined, highly lamellar microstructure with an increased β‐phase aspect ratio.
fields.conditions: Isothermal oxidation testing at 1200°C under controlled cyclic oxidation conditions, with identical compositions aside from the processing route.
fields.structural_mediator: Increased lamellar β‐phase aspect ratio that reduces the effective PL, thereby lowering the critical Al concentration for maintaining exclusive Al2O3 formation on the surface.
fields.mechanism: A higher aspect ratio of the β‐phase limits the number of phase boundaries per unit length, effectively reducing the local Al-depletion rate and aiding rapid formation of a continuous Al2O3 scale. The reduction in phase intersections mitigates Al flux discrepancies and local compositional heterogeneities, slowing further oxide growth and improving scale adherence.
fields.predicted_outcome: Samples with a tailored high-aspect-ratio lamellar structure will exhibit lower oxidation rate constants and thinner, more coherent oxide scales (with reduced spallation) relative to the baseline, with improvements potentially on the order of an additional 20-30% reduction in oxidation kinetics, within the uncertainty of scale formation kinetics.
fields.baseline: The performance of the arc-melted MPEA with the original eutectic microstructure, as characterized in the paper.
fields.boundary: This hypothesis should hold for alloys where the phase chemistry and overall composition remain in the eutectic regime; if the β-phase becomes too scarce or if the aspect ratio cannot be meaningfully increased, the effect may not be observed.
fields.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in oxidation rate constants depend on the achievable aspect ratios and may vary; detailed thermal profiles during directional solidification must be optimized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of MPEA samples: one using conventional arc melting and one using directional solidification to obtain a high-aspect-ratio lamellar structure. Expose both to identical oxidation testing at 1200°C for 500 h.
measurements: Oxidation rate constant (kp) via mass gain measurements.
TGO thickness and morphology using cross-sectional SEM/TEM.
Assessment of spallation via cyclic oxidation area loss measurements.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the directionally solidified samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >15-20% improvement) in oxidation rate constant and TGO spallation relative to the baseline, the hypothesis would be falsified.

top3.label: C6
top3.builds_on: The in situ HTXRD observations from the paper that revealed a layered oxide scale with a Mn-rich top and Cr-rich inner layer.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis extends the paper’s findings by proposing an active compositional/process intervention to deliberately enhance the beneficial Cr-rich inner layer, thereby directly linking dual-layer oxide formation to improved long-term oxidation resistance in harsh high-temperature environments.

fields.hypothesis: In CrMnFeCoNi‐based multiprincipal‐element alloys, oxidation resistance and material integrity are governed by the formation of a dual-layer oxide scale consisting of an outer Mn-rich oxide and an inner, adherent Cr-rich (or Cr-enriched) layer that acts as a diffusion barrier to oxygen and further metal migration.
fields.material_initial_state: Homogenized, arc‐melted and annealed CrMnFeCoNi HEA with an equiatomic composition and FCC solid-solution structure.
fields.intervention: Modify oxidation conditions by controlling oxygen partial pressure and/or slightly increasing the relative Cr activity (e.g., through minor controlled alloying or heat-treatment driven segregation) to promote a thicker, more continuous Cr-rich inner layer during high-temperature oxidation.
fields.conditions: High-temperature oxidation in air from ~550 °C to 1100 °C, maintaining a controlled oxygen environment that encourages selective oxidation kinetics.
fields.structural_mediator: A stratified oxide scale with a non-protective Mn-rich outer zone and a protective, adherent Cr-rich inner layer that limits further oxygen ingress.
fields.mechanism: At high temperatures, Mn – the most reactive element – rapidly diffuses to the surface to form a Mn oxide that initially grows quickly but is non-protective. A modest increase in Cr activity can enhance the formation of a continuous Cr-rich oxide layer beneath the Mn oxide. This Cr-rich inner scale, due to its lower ionic diffusivity and denser structure, serves as an effective barrier that slows further oxidation and protects the underlying metal. This dual-layer mechanism integrates the ‘sluggish kinetic diffusion effect’ noted in high-entropy alloys and the protective nature of dense oxide scales [PMC10384371::web::003, PMC10384371::web::021].
fields.predicted_outcome: The modified alloy will exhibit lower overall oxidation rates (e.g., reduced weight gain and slower parabolic oxidation kinetics) compared to the baseline, with in situ XRD showing earlier and more pronounced reflections from a Cr-rich phase layer and reduced Mn oxide spallation.
fields.baseline: Unmodified CrMnFeCoNi alloy that predominantly forms a Mn-rich oxide scale with limited inner barrier formation, as observed in the in situ HTXRD studies.
fields.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in environments ranging from moderate to high oxygen partial pressures and temperatures between ~550 °C and 1100 °C.
fields.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of Cr layer formation and its ultimate impact on long-term oxidation resistance may vary with small compositional changes and thermal histories.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi samples: one as the baseline and another with a modified processing route (or minor compositional tweak) designed to enhance Cr surface segregation. Expose both sets to high-temperature oxidation in air (550 °C to 1100 °C) under identical oxygen partial pressure and time profiles with in situ XRD monitoring of oxide phase evolution.
measurements: In situ XRD to monitor phase formation and transformation kinetics.
Weight gain measurements to quantify oxidation rate.
Surface microscopy (SEM/EDS) to verify oxide scale layer composition and structure.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples engineered to promote a Cr-rich inner layer do not demonstrate a significantly reduced oxidation rate or fail to exhibit a well-defined, adherent Cr-rich oxide barrier compared with the baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.
